label: Constitutional amendment (photo ID for all voters)
t: Photo ID for all voters, including mail voters
what: Amends Article VI so that all voters, not only those voting in person, must present photo identification before voting. The constitution has required photo ID for in-person voting since 2018; mail voters currently send a copy of an ID (or an exception form) under state law.
y: The constitution requires photo ID from every voter, including absentee/mail voters.
n: The constitutional photo ID rule continues to cover only in-person voting; mail-ballot ID rules stay in statute.
pro: Sen. Warren Daniel (R), former Sen. Paul Newton (R), legislative Republicans
con: Democracy North Carolina, Rep. Mary Harrison (D), most legislative Democrats

label: Constitutional amendment (income tax rate cap)
t: Lower the income tax rate cap from 7% to 3.5%
what: Lowers the maximum state income tax rate allowed by the constitution, for both personal and corporate income, from 7% to 3.5% for tax years starting on or after January 1, 2027. It does not change today's rates: the personal rate is 3.99% in 2026 and, under a 2023 law, is projected to fall to 3.49% in 2027 and 2.99% in 2028 as revenue triggers are met.
y: A future legislature could not raise the income tax rate above 3.5% without another constitutional amendment.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Research Division: no fiscal impact, because personal rates are projected at 3.49% (2027) and 2.99% (2028+) and the corporate rate falls to 0% by 2030. If revenue missed the 2025-26 trigger, the 3.99% rate would apply and the cap would force a cut. Referendum costs minimal.
pro: Sen. Michael Lee (R), Sen. Lisa Barnes (R), Sen. Benton Sawrey (R), legislative Republicans
con: Gov. Josh Stein (D), NC Budget & Tax Center, legislative Democrats

reasons.fiscal: Fiscal Research expects no near-term impact, but notes the cap would force a rate cut below 3.99% if revenue triggers were missed, narrowing future revenue options.

label: Constitutional amendment (property tax levy limit)
t: Require limits on local property tax increases
what: Requires the General Assembly to pass general laws limiting how much a local government's property tax levy may increase, which may include exceptions. The size of the limit and how it is measured are not set by the amendment; they would come in later legislation.
y: Lawmakers must enact a cap on growth in county, city and other local property tax levies.
n: No constitutional requirement to cap local property tax levy growth.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Research Division: no fiscal impact, because the limit's details would be set by future legislation (to get its own fiscal note). For context, county and municipal property tax revenue rose 8.1% to $15.1B in FY2024-25.
pro: Rep. Brian Echevarria (R), House Speaker Destin Hall (R), Rep. Alan Branson (R)
con: NC Budget & Tax Center, Rep. Deb Butler (D)
